reading.body:
Sega v. Accolade holds that copying a program in full is fair use when that copy is the only way to reach unprotected functional elements and there is a legitimate reason to reach them.

The doctrine it anchors is intermediate copying: the copy made along the way is judged by what it was for, not by the fact that it was complete. Training pipelines depend on this because ingestion necessarily makes copies before any output exists. The case is cited for intermediate copying, reverse engineering, and interoperability.

The limit is explicit. Accolade needed the copy to achieve interoperability, a purpose the court treated as legitimate and narrow. Whether producing a competing creative work is the same kind of purpose is exactly what is now contested. Eight live cases are listed against this precedent, including UMG Recordings v. Suno and Vredenburgh v. OpenAI, within a total of 90 live cases.
